en: The Introductory Discourse on the Jewel Mirror Commentary to the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, composed by the Śramaṇa Pǔwěn of Gānglíng, who was granted the title "Lecturer at Fājìe Monastery in Yúnnán" by Imperial Decree during the Dàqīng Dynasty.

It is truly the case that the fundamental principles of the Sage’s teachings originate from a single thread; yet, to follow them like one seeking a sheep by its tracks leads only to much self-delusion.
Thus, the clouds of delusion spread across the ocean of enlightenment, and dark mists arise within the clear void.

Consequently, the gates of the magnificent mansion are perpetually sealed by thorns and brambles, such that the Tathāgata-garbha remains forever locked away from the ignorant and foolish. Reflecting deeply upon the Buddha’s words, they are perfectly clear;
it is only a pity that human interpretations have gone astray. Having deviated from the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), they have further misled beginners. Therefore, I have often...
Facing the moon upon my meditation cushion, I held the scroll and read its texts among the rocks and pines; I could not restrain my deep sighs.

Thus, for twenty years I have savored and relished it, investigating it at midnight and exhaustively searching through the finest commentaries to directly explore the essential purport of the original scripture.
My endeavor lies in reverently embodying the Sage’s intent so as to harmonize with the scriptural texts, clearly demonstrating the Great Samādhi and elucidating the nature of the mind.

This is merely like adding flowers upon brocade, or briefly removing a speck of dust from before one's eyes. Having composed this commentary, I first set forth this introductory preface, received and upheld [the teachings].

O Worthy One, I shall present ten general gateways: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, its inclusion within the divisions of the Piṭakas and Vehicles; third, the delimitation of the teachings and their meanings;

fourth, the appropriate capacities of those to be taught; fifth, the essential nature of that which expresses; sixth, the fundamental tenets and ultimate purpose of that which is expressed; seventh, the chronological sequence of the traces of the teaching;
eighth, the dates of the transmission and translation; ninth, a general explanation of the title; and tenth, a detailed interpretation of the textual meaning.
First, regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching: whenever ordinary people in the world undertake any matter, there is invariably a purposeful cause and condition;
how much more so for the Great Teaching of the Buddha—how could it have arisen without such a reason? There are two types of causes and conditions: first, the general; second, the specific.

"Totality" refers to repaying causes and responding to requests, manifesting the principle and delivering sentient beings; the emergence of the teachings throughout the entire lifetime of the Buddha all proceeds from this.

Examining the Buddha’s original intent, it was solely for the sake of the one great causal event (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*): he desired to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).
Yet, although this knowledge and vision is inherently possessed by sentient beings, they are deluded and do not know it themselves; thus, they sink into the cycle of birth and death.
Death. The Buddha realized this principle while still within the realm of causes; he made a vow to attain Buddhahood and universally manifest it to all sentient beings.

Therefore, although the various teachings of the five periods contain explanations of provisional and real, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect, or indeterminate, their fundamental intent is solely for the sake of the One Great Matter.
This constitutes the general causal condition for all teachings. Specifically, there are...
Ten: first, to encourage and advance extensive learning; second, to clearly demonstrate true concentration;
third, to distinguish between the real and the false; fourth, to directly point to the human mind; fifth, to uproot craving and desire; sixth, to firmly maintain pure precepts;
seventh, to skillfully show the gates of cultivation; eighth, to provide stages for realization and entry; ninth, to resolve doubts and warn against stagnation; tenth, to...
This work clarifies the correct and refutes the heterodox.

First, it is intended to encourage those who possess extensive learning; secondly, it is for those whose extensive learning has led them astray, serving as a warning against wild wisdom so that they may be inspired toward authentic practice.
This is because this sutra was initiated at a site of sexual misconduct, using that as the opening to provide exhortation and guidance. From [this point]...

When the Venerable One returned from the chamber of desire, he immediately said: "I regret that since beginningless time, I have been devoted solely to extensive learning, yet have not fully perfected the power of the Way.
I earnestly entreat the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means by which they attained the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi.
Thereupon, the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Even if you were able to memorize and uphold the twelve..."
The pure and wondrous principles of the various sections of the sūtras are not equal to cultivating untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for even a single day. Mañjuśrī also said:
"If you can hear what is heard by all Buddhas, why do you not hear that which hears? Therefore, the treatise states:

Although Ānanda had extensively heard, upheld, and mastered the various sūtras of the twelve divisions, his wisdom was great while his mental concentration was slight; thus, he once encountered the calamity of the *Taṅga* (Dharmadinnā) and [forgot] the twelve divisions of the sūtras.
Having maintained these through accumulated kalpas, they are like water poured from a jar, or like the wind and a shadow—utterly unreliable.

Only then did he reproach himself for his lack of merit, turn his mind toward seeking meditative concentration, and request it. Had it not been for Mahāpajāpatī Gautamī’s single act of summoning and gathering him, Ānanda would still have remained submerged in the ocean of the treasury of much-hearing;
even after passing through kalpas, he would have remained as he was, and might not have been able to so fiercely and incisively break through his habitual tendencies through cultivation.

It is untainted (*anāsrava*). The reason this account of the learned man (*bahuśruta*) is presented as the causal narrative (*nidāna*) is precisely to serve as a model of admonition for the intelligent people of future generations.
Thus, the Tathāgata exerted himself to emit light from the crown of his head to eliminate craving and preach the "Crown Dharma" (*uṣṇīṣa-dharma*) to pull them from the mire of desire.
He universally shattered the sturdy gates of the great earth and instantly released the shackles of humans and devas. If...

It is said: "Use poison to counteract poison. Thus, the evil mantra serves as a catalyst for progress; the animal’s hearing and its turning back toward hearing serve as the very guide for the harlot’s cultivation.
In short, this demonstrates that mere hearing is ineffective, while encouraging true cultivation is beneficial.
For this reason, he preached this sutra. Second, regarding the specific demonstration of true samādhi: It is because when...
The faculties were thus gathered. Because there was no true samādhi, Miaoshan’s request was made, and the Buddha granted it, saying:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the path of wondrous adornment by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.
This demonstrates true samādhi. Indeed, regarding both the mundane and supramundane realms, all...

Externally, the provisional and the small [vehicles] each have their fixed [teachings]. Yet, they lack ultimate realization because the essential substance upon which they rely is entirely the mind of birth-and-death consciousness, rather than the true mind that is beyond birth and death. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of the discrimination of dharma-objects. This is because...
Among all humans and devas, those who first cultivate meditative concentration have not yet attained definitive discernment; there are few who do not rely upon this mind.

Even regarding the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, though one may exert oneself in diligent study, one cannot transcend this. Furthermore, it is said: "When all discrimination is absent, it is neither form nor emptiness.
Those such as Kuśarī mistake this for the *tattva* (the obscure principle). This, then, is the view of all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The false concentrations they cultivate also employ this mind. Furthermore, it is said that although all those in the world who practice the various stages of training may manifest the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), they fail to exhaust their outflows and become Arhats because they all cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality.
From this, one knows that all those of provisional or limited capacity likewise employ this [mind].

Therefore, Ānanda said: "If this luminous manifestation were not the mind, I would be without a mind, identical to wood or earth. Furthermore, there was no one among this great assembly who was not struck with alarm and doubt.
Based on this, it follows that all ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or limited vehicles [are likewise without such a mind].

There are none who do not grasp this as the true mind. Yet, if one wishes to cultivate this true samādhi, one must first eliminate the deluded consciousness of arising and ceasing and necessarily recognize the true mind.
For this reason, the Buddha points out the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth within the sense faculties;
he even uses gestures such as raising his fist, bending his fingers, and moving light to the left and right to bring together the three categories and harmonize the seven elements.

Whether by means of the sound of the bell or the resonance of the pestle, it is none other than to manifest this true mind—which is all-pervasive, perfectly interfused, eternally constant, immovable, unborn, and undying.

Therefore, at the end of the fourth fascicle, it says: "If one abandons birth and death to maintain the constant radiance, once the constant radiance manifests before one, the faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and the mind will dissolve accordingly. Conceptual appearances become dust, and the consciousness-emotion..."
These are defilements. When both are abandoned, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright; how then could you fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
Furthermore, the essence of this samādhi is precisely the eternally abiding true mind, the inherently pure and luminous substance.
Even if one were to compose ten volumes of profound prose, to speak of its essentials, it is unified solely in this one samādhi. Therefore, the beginning of the sutra says: "There is samādhi."
It is titled "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King," and so forth; thus one knows that it encompasses and governs all samādhis.
Therefore, the monk of Wujiang’s designation of this as "the general dharma-gate of the entire sutra" is truly profound.

This is evident in the tenfold demonstration that follows, as well as in the three categories and seven elements, all of which are described as being fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

This correctly points to the true essence of the wondrous samādhi. Thus, Ānanda and the great assembly each came to know for themselves that the essence of mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions;
they viewed emptiness as a mere leaf and regarded their bodies as but dust, thereby gaining correct faith in the principle of true samādhi.

This elucidates the essence of true samādhi. Even in the chapter on Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, it reveals the continuous arising of the myriad dharmas and the perfect interfusion of the five great elements, fully manifesting the three baskets (Tripitaka).
The great assembly thereby gains benefit, correctly understanding the principle of true samādhi and attaining its essence.
Following the middle of the fourth fascicle, it clarifies the two certainties regarding the initial aspiration for enlightenment.

Regarding the meaning: through the practice of the three-week period, the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared, and the twenty-five sages each expounded their realization of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
This demonstrates the practice of true samādhi by means of both primary and auxiliary matters.
From the twelve classes of living beings to the three gradual steps, fifty-five stages are established; this further reveals the truth by means of the phenomena of delusion and enlightenment.

This is the verification of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As for the end of the sutra, the five layers of the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) refer to the delusive objects encountered throughout concentration.
From this it can be known that what is discussed as "faith and understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) throughout the entire sutra is the essential substance (*dharmatā*) of true concentration.
"Practicing and realizing" refers to the functional application of true samādhi. One must therefore know that if one seeks true samādhi, one must recognize the true mind;
yet, simply recognizing the true mind is itself termed true samādhi. Thus, the Sūtra says: "For example, it is like the lute, the harp, and the *konghou*."
This refers to the fact that although there may be a wondrous sound, if there are no wondrous fingers, it can ultimately never be produced.
It is precisely for this reason that the Buddha preached this sutra in order to point out true samādhi. Third, regarding the discernment between the real and the false:
"discern" (jian) means to eliminate the false; "distinguish" (bie) means to differentiate the real. This refers to the two kinds of fundamental natures in this very sutra. As it says:

What are these two kinds? First is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is that which you now take as your own nature—the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the攀緣心 or攀緣心, the mind that clings to and discriminates objects).

Second is the fundamentally pure essence of beginningless bodhi and nirvana, which is your current *shí-jīng* (識精, the essence of consciousness), the original luminosity capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet that which is overlooked by those very conditions. This is the Buddha’s demonstration of the true [nature] for the sake of the practitioner.
Delusion is the root. However, to distinguish between them, it is impossible unless one skillfully employs the two gates of equality and expedient means.
What is meant by equality? It is because all phenomena originally stem from the single mind.

Since there is but the single mind, all differentiated aspects of cultivation and realization—whether true or false, substantial or insubstantial, deviant or correct, right or wrong—are fundamentally non-existent.
It is so called because it is attained as equality. What is the skillful means? Although the principle is one, phenomena differ in a thousand ways;
therefore, within the midst of all dharmas, one may manifest the true and refute the false, distinguish the correct and expel the heterodox, and affirm what is right while rejecting what is wrong.

It is called "expedient means" (*upāya*) because it clarifies cultivation, reveals the truth, and provides realization. Therefore, the Tathāgata employs two gates in tandem: first, he uses expedient means to discern the true from the false;
beginning with the refutation of the deluded consciousness in its seven locations, he concludes with the refutation of the notion that [the nature of seeing] is not a composite.
Thus, regarding consciousness, he definitively refutes it as being false and causes one to abandon it; regarding the nature of seeing, he definitively reveals it.

That which is true is made to be grasped; this is the gate of skillful means. Now that both the true and the delusive have been clarified and the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* has been revealed, if it were restricted solely to the sense organs and not harmonized with the myriad dharmas, how could it be called the "Perfect and Wondrous Great Samādhi"?
Therefore, next, through equality, the true and the delusive are universally fused, beginning first with the reconciliation of the four [elements].

The *kō* (sections) traverse the seven great categories, ultimately culminating in the full manifestation of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*). When one universally scrutinizes thought and deliberation, even the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) cannot be excluded;
how then could consciousness (*vijñāna*) be selective? This is because, fundamentally, there is not a single dharma that can be divided into the real and the false;
this is what is called the "Gate of Equality. Nevertheless, these two gates are like essence and function: they support and assist one another, and must not be treated as partial or biased.
This is what is meant by "abandonment. If expedient means (*upāya*) are not established, then truth and falsehood will be confused, and right and wrong cannot be distinguished;
how, then, can one penetrate the essence to perceive the Truth? If impartiality is lacking, then truth and falsehood will remain eternally separated, and right and wrong will be manifest;

how could such a state be called "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*) or "wondrous" (*miao*)? Therefore, when discussing the nature (*dhātu*), one must be proficient in these two gates; only then does it become perfect and wondrous. Thus did the Buddha [teach].
To reveal the true and shatter the false, and to harmonize the false with the true—showing these two gates—the Buddha preached this sutra.

△ Fourth, regarding "directly pointing to the human mind": this refers to the Buddha’s indication, at the gateway of the six sense faculties of sentient beings, of the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth;
this is precisely the eternally abiding true mind. For this reason, when the assembly first requested the samādhi, the Buddha first examined them.
Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta: since the source of attachment and views has already been set forth, and one is entirely deluded regarding the essence of reality, it is explained as follows:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of purity and luminosity.
They employ various false thoughts; because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic transmigration. It further says: "This..."
"True wondrous clarity" is precisely the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana.
When the interlocutor reproached himself for not knowing the quiescent and eternal, the Tathāgata granted that he could give rise to the "wondrously clear mind.
Therefore, within the interlocutor’s own present body, [the Buddha] pointed out the nature of seeing, saying: "This is the mind, not the eye. This single sentence alone is already perfectly clear.

He pointed his finger. Yet it was as if he were performing human affairs with his mouth. Thus, in the "Chapter on Immovability," when the Tathāgata bent his fingers and flashed light from left to right, this was precisely a face-to-face presentation.
At that moment, for one who is ready to receive the teaching, one first recognizes the immovable master at the gateway of the six sense faculties.
Therefore, he accepted the encounter with words filling his mouth. This is not only the case here; it is also so in what preceded.
In the passage "Breaking Through Consciousness," he raises his fist and shows it to us; with a single "Hah! he seeks the mind.
This is indeed a case where the seal and the gesture race together, transcending both words and thought. Viewed in this light, what single word is not a direct pointing to the human mind?
What single place is not where one may see one's nature and become a Buddha? In sum, the Tathāgata clarifies the essence through the teachings; he does not look to the faces of others.
Tracing this back through the generations to later times, when the classification of teachings (*jiaopan*) became the primary concern, it evolved into a secondary gate of meaning.

Consequently, it could not avoid falling into the ranks of the blind; for they established their own boundaries between the Tathāgata-dhyāna and the Patriarchal-dhyāna, falsely distinguishing between them as superior or inferior.
This is like the case of Rāhula striking the bell later on to let [the monk] verify it for himself, or making the sleeping man experience the dream of the pestle, thereby causing him to...

"Self-knowledge. These are all the Tathāgata’s thorough overturning of the foundation, his placing of the entire platter upon the table; they are a brand-new decree, possessing extraordinary brilliance and edge.
They represent the total presentation of both killing and giving life—the very point of directly pointing to the human mind.

Therefore, know that this sutra is consistent from beginning to end, pointing solely to the human mind and containing nothing else. Thus, when the occasion arose, he made the formal request for the wondrous samādhi. The world...

Venerable sir, you first inquire about the arousal of the bodhicitta; desiring that faith be generated, you extensively refute [the misconceptions regarding] the seven locations, reveal the ten instances, and harmonize the four categories to perfectly manifest the seven elements, thereby clarifying the entire substance of the true mind that pervades the Dharma-realm.
Desiring that understanding be opened, you clarify the causes for the continuity of birth and the principle of perfect interfusion, showing how the single mind constitutes the myriad dharmas.
All phenomena are gathered and returned to the single mind; thus, the single mind reveals the fundamental substance of all phenomena.

Yet, when one wishes to demonstrate this through practice, both the primary and auxiliary methods are clarified, each describing its own path of perfect penetration. Ultimately, the nature of hearing alone is selected, and the mantra-heart is expounded once more.
Whether exoteric or esoteric teachings are presented, they are all nothing other than means to support and stimulate the wondrous function of this mind.

Furthermore, when he wishes to demonstrate [the truth] through proof, he engages them in discourse on delusion and enlightenment, discusses defilement and purity, transforms the various classes of beings, and establishes the stages of sagehood;
all of these are the manifest great functions of this mind. This is precisely what is reiterated in the "Chapter on Repeated Explanations," where he discusses the seven destinies.
Thus, they originate from the internal and external divisions of the mind. To discern the five māras is to follow the mind’s affectionate thoughts and perverse reflections.

One should know that all that is expounded in the sutras—whether defiled or pure, whether sacred or mundane, even including the true and the false, the perverse and the correct, the conditioned and the spontaneous—all is the mind; there is no other dharma apart from it, as it points directly to the truth.
Qian: Could there indeed be anything that surpasses this? Thus we know that the Tathāgata preached this sutra in order to point directly to the human mind.
△ Fifth, for the purpose of uprooting greed and desire: This is because the continuity of sentient beings all arises from greed and desire as the cause;
the cycle of rebirth in the seven realms of existence is equally based upon emotional attachments and conceptualizations. Therefore, one should know that among the four modes of birth and the six...
Whether in the heavens or among humans, although there are differences in rising and falling, all alike return to birth and death without distinction.
If one seeks the reason for this, it is none other than being struck by the poisoned arrow of craving, desire, and emotional attachment. Therefore it is said:
"All sentient beings take lustful desire as the very basis of their life and nature. If lustful desire is not severed, then birth and death cannot be avoided.
Those who wish to transcend birth and death must eliminate lustful desire. Therefore, I, the Tathāgata, universally desire that all sentient beings shall completely remove this arrow.
Thus, because my beloved younger brother mistakenly fell into a chamber of lust, I emitted the light of fearlessness from the invisible crown of my head.
The Buddha of the Present Unconditioned has preached this unsurpassed mantra. Yet, were it not for one of great wisdom, it would be impossible to extract the poisonous arrows of emotional desire.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī was dispatched with the mantra to go and protect [the practitioner], pouring forth this cool, refreshing nectar directly into the midst of the blazing fire-pit.
Thus, Daṅgā’s lustful mind finally ceased, and the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) was established within the recipient.
Having fully [subdued them], he then rouses and encourages them, causing them to return to the Buddha’s presence.
Thus, the lustful woman Pūtanā dried up the river of craving and became a forest of diligence within the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, together with Yaśodharā, she awakened to their past causes;
realizing that craving is suffering, they both attained the fruit of sainthood. Thus, the fetter of attachment was forever severed and sexual misconduct forever abandoned—this is precisely the skull.
Powdery grime is instantly transformed into fragrant light; the lustful body and mind are fully realized as the fruit of sainthood.

This is the true mirror for severing lust and escaping birth and death. However, in this very sutra, the beginning and end are explained in detail, all taking the departure from desire as the essential point.
Thus, when the audience beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs, they immediately remarked that these features could not have arisen from the love of desire.
[They] are born. Why is this? Because the vital energy of desire is coarse, turbid, and foul;

it is a chaotic mixture of pus and blood, unable to give rise to the supreme, pure, wondrously bright, and purple-golden mass of light. For this reason, they yearn with thirst and reverence, shaving their heads and leaving the household life under the Buddha.

As for the passage in the chapter on Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra concerning the continuity of sentient beings, it says: "Thought and craving are bound together; because of craving, one cannot be separated."
Thus, throughout all the worlds, parents and children are born one after another in an unbroken succession; these are rooted in desire and greed.
Even the four kinds of clear instructions state at their outset: "If the sentient beings of the six realms do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; yet if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you remain in the dust.

One must not depart from this. Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lustful desire, they will inevitably fall into the paths of demons.
Among the ten causes of habitual practice, the habit of lust is placed first; by the time of the sixfold mutual retribution, it is clearly evident that the retribution for desire is the most severe.
Therefore, among the three poisons, craving and desire are the most poisonous; and among all forms of decay, female form is the most destructive.
Decay. Therefore, those who encounter it cannot fail to lose their Dharma-body and wound their wisdom-life; they sink into birth and death and undergo saṃsāra.
Alas, how poisonous this is! Such is the nature of this arrow. Thus, Mañjuśrī exhorted the one ready for the teaching, saying:
"If you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, your accumulation of learning will become a source of error. Judging from this, [the problem] is manifold.
Even those who have heard the teachings and possess wisdom, if they are pierced by this arrow even once, will find no ground for progress and will instead fall into error;

how much more so for the ignorant masses and the "dumb sheep" who have not heard the Dharma? Thus, within the seven realms of existence, beings are distinguished as ascending or falling according to their thoughts and perceptions;
yet within the five aggregates, it is through craving and desire that Māra is identified. Therefore, one who wishes to practice cultivation—
True Samādhi. First, one must eliminate the mind of lust. If one does not sever lust, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra;
thus, Potalaka fell into hell because of his secret transgressions, while Ucchuṣma attained realization of the Truth through the cultivation of revulsion.

For this reason, the Tathāgata preached this sūtra in order to remove the arrow of greed and desire. △ Sixth, for those who firmly uphold the pure precepts: although the primary purport of this sūtra...
It clarifies that concentration and wisdom must be cultivated in equal measure. If one lacks pure precepts as a foundation, then concentration and wisdom will likewise be difficult to achieve.

For this reason, throughout the beginning and end of the sutra, the Tathāgata repeatedly and earnestly elucidates this point; it is nothing other than his desire for people to maintain pure precepts while cultivating concentration and wisdom.
Therefore, at the opening chapter concerning the testimony of faith, the compiler of the sutra first describes the strict purification of the *vinaya*.
Modeling himself after the three realms, he spoke of falling into error through the arousal [of afflictions], saying, "One will destroy the essence of the precepts.
Yet, when reaching the section on Practice within the Main Text of the *Zhengzong*, there is originally no separate method; the Buddha merely declared:
"You have often heard me proclaim in the *Vinaya* the three principles of definitive practice for cultivation: namely, to take the gathering of the mind as the precept, and based upon the precept..."

Birth is fixed by concentration; from concentration, wisdom is produced. These are called the three untainted trainings (*trīṇy aśaikṣāṇi*). Furthermore, it is said: "What is the gathering of the mind?
I call this 'precept' (*śīla*). If the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful thoughts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
Even when you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, you must first sever the mind [of lust]."
Sexual misconduct—this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.
Furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
Thus, when you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, you must next sever the taking of life; this is called the Tathāgata’s [instruction from] the Buddhas of the past.

This is the World-Honored One’s second definitive instruction on purity. Furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms within the world, if their minds do not steal, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.

Thus, when you instruct the people of the world to practice samādhi, they must subsequently sever the act of stealing; this is called the third definitive instruction on purity from the former Buddhas and World-Honored Ones.

Jingming said further: "In this world, although the sentient beings of the six realms may have no killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, and thus these three practices may be perfected, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity;
they will become demons of craving and views and lose the seed of the Tathāgata. This applies even to you who teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, yet later..."
To sever all great falsehoods is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddha of former kalpas.

Furthermore, regarding the demonstration and realization within the three gradual stages—eliminating auxiliary causes, excising the fundamental nature, and reversing manifest karma—it is none other than by relying on this that one first attains it;
through the middle-of-the-middle flow, the fifty-five stages are all achieved by means of this.
Thus, one should know that the precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed bodhi; one ought to maintain the pure precepts with a single-minded resolve.
Regarding the chapter on the seven destinies: the wholesome paths of humans and devas arise from the precepts and wholesome deeds through which one ascends by leaving desire behind;

whereas the remaining evil destinies result from the loss of precepts and wholesome deeds and the indulgence of desire, through which one falls. For this reason, the māras of the five aggregates seek only to destroy and disparage [the precepts].
The precepts cause sentient beings to fall into doubt and error; they single-mindedly slander pure bhikṣus who uphold the precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna path.
Thus, one should know that praise is the mark of the worthy and noble, while slander is that of demons and malevolent spirits.

Therefore, all who wish to cultivate the wondrous wisdom of the nature-emptiness samādhi must first maintain these precepts, as pure as ice and frost. Reciting the heart-mantra together with this practice establishes the foundation for entering samādhi.

Each can serve as the essence [of the teaching]. The former [the preceding passage] generally encompasses the expressed essence (*abhidheya-svabhāva*);
the above was the literal text (*vyañjana*), whereas this belongs to the meaning (*artha*). Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In all sūtras..."
The essence [of the teaching] briefly consists of two kinds: first, the text; second, the meaning. The text is that which expresses, while the meaning belongs to that which is expressed.

Therefore, text and meaning follow one another and are not separate; only when they are thus combined does the essence of the teaching as a conforming phenomenon (lakṣaṇānuvartin) come to be established.

Second is the gate of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra). This means that the aforementioned two essences are both inseparable from consciousness, because all that exists is a manifestation of mind alone.
Nevertheless, there are also two [aspects]. First, the mutual correspondence between the original and the reflection; second, the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener.

Regarding the first, within the section on the original and the reflection, if one follows Qingliang (Chengguan), four propositions are established by applying them across the five teachings: 1. Only the original exists, without a reflection.

This refers to the Hīnayāna, because they do not understand *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). 2. Both the original and the reflection exist. This refers to the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, namely, the Buddha...
The proclamation of both the words and their meaning is that which is manifested by the pure consciousness associated with the Tathāgata’s wondrous discerning wisdom;
this is called the teaching of fundamental wisdom. As for the listener, it refers to the words and meanings transformed upon their own consciousness.
This is called "image" (*pratibimba*). Third, there is "only image without a basis," which refers to the Mahāyāna’s teaching of ultimate reality—that is, the teaching of suchness (*tathatā*).

It asserts that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature and that all things are suchness; there remains only the principle of suchness (*tathatā-nyāya*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) alone.
With great compassion and great wisdom acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they manifest the Buddha within the minds of those to be converted whose faculties have matured.
The teaching through forms and sounds is therefore merely a reflection within the minds of sentient beings.

The fourth [category], which is neither the original nor a reflection, is the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna. This means that it is not only the case that there are no forms or sounds of the Buddha outside the mind;
rather, even the reflections within the minds of sentient beings are empty. This is the teaching beyond teachings, wherein words are forgotten and thoughts are severed. Thus, Vimalakīrti...
It is said: "As for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no showing; as for those who listen to the Dharma, there is no hearing and no attainment. This is it.

Combining the preceding four explanations into one whole is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This refers to what is known as perfect interfusion without obstruction, where the original and its reflection are both fused, thereby encompassing all sentient beings.
Next, within the context of preaching and listening, this is further divided into two parts. The first concerns their identity.

The teachings are established through four propositions. Second, regarding the Separate Teaching (biejiao), they are likewise established through four propositions. △ First, concerning the four teachings sharing the same proposition:
this clarifies the meaning of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) by means of the mutual dissolution of sentient beings and Buddhas.

First, outside the true mind of the Buddha, there are no separate sentient beings, because the true mind of sentient beings is precisely the true mind of the Buddha. Thus, there is only the speaker and no listener.

Therefore, the teachings that are spoken are manifested solely by the Buddha. Second, apart from the minds of sentient beings, there is no separate Buddha, because the true mind of the Buddha is identical to the true mind of sentient beings;
thus, these are merely heard and not spoken. Therefore, the teachings that are spoken are manifested solely by sentient beings themselves.
Third, when the true mind of the Buddha manifests, it does not obstruct the manifestation of the true mind of sentient beings; therefore, they are said [to be spoken].

Listen with dual fusion. Both are simultaneously extinguished. Since the four Buddhas are identical to sentient beings, they are not Buddhas; since sentient beings are identical to the Buddhas, they are not beings.
When both are mutually negated and vanish, then both speaking and listening are quiescent. Second, clarifying the four propositions of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
This uses the mutual existence of sentient beings and Buddhas to clarify the meaning of the Separate Teaching. First: Sentient beings are entirely present within the Buddha-mind.

1. Because [the Buddha] is within [sentient beings], the phenomena subsumed under the aspect of the fruit (phala) are complete without exception. Since sentient beings still abide within the Buddha’s mind, how much more so the teachings he proclaims—they cannot fail to be manifestations of the Buddha’s mind.
2. Because the Buddha abides within the minds of sentient beings, the phenomena subsumed under the aspect of the cause (hetu) are complete without exception.

Since the Buddha still abides within the minds of beings, how much more so the teachings he proclaims—they cannot fail to be manifestations of the minds of beings. 3. By virtue of [the identity of] sentient beings and the Buddha...
As they exist together and each is real rather than false, cause and effect interpenetrate. According to the sacred teachings, the entirety [of reality] resides within these two minds.
Thus, the Buddha within the mind of sentient beings preaches the Dharma for the sake of the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind;

the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind listen to the Dharma preached by the Buddha within their own minds. Since the four modes of birth are entirely present within the Buddha, they are identical to the Buddha. This is...
When the Buddha is fully present within birth, then he shares that same birth; thus, the two aspects are established once more, and cause and effect are manifested together.

In all discourse, both speaker and listener are simultaneously identical and distinct. However, when one realizes that within the mind of the Buddha there are no sentient beings to hear, and within the minds of sentient beings there is no Buddha to speak, then one knows that this sutra returns to the state of non-attainment. Only when both identity and distinction are encompassed can it be considered ultimate.

End. Profoundly Deep Consciousness-Only. △ Third, the Gate of Returning to Nature (*xing*). Xianshou says: "This gathers the eight consciousnesses that are manifested back into the single mind that manifests them;
this is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. Therefore, it is called 'returning to nature. △ Fourth, the Gate of Non-obstruction. Xianshou states:
"Within the first three gates, the mind and its objects, principle and phenomena, are a single *paratantra* arising. They are blended together.

Fusion is unimpeded; they interpenetrate and mutually encompass one another to constitute the essence of the teaching. This is because the single dharma of the One Mind has two gates, each of which encompasses all dharmas.
Thus, the gate of arising and ceasing subsumes the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) of phenomenal characteristics, while the gate of True Suchness subsumes the return to the fundamental nature.
Consequently, in the former gate, the mind and its objects are unimpeded, and in the latter gate, principle and phenomena are unimpeded.

It is unimpeded. Therefore, although Qingliang extensively expounded the gates of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*) and the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*), he ultimately converged them back into the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*hai-yin sanmei*), thereby exhausting the full purport of non-obstruction.

Thus, since this sutra properly belongs to the Final Teaching (*zhong-jiao*) while also encompassing the Sudden and Perfect Teachings, it fully accords with the categories of the entire body of the teachings as established by Xianshou and Qingliang.

"Yun" (允) means "to accord with. The sixth [section] concerns the tenets (*zong*) and their ultimate goals (*qu*) as elucidated therein. This refers to what Xianshou termed "tenet" (*zong*), meaning that which is venerated by a particular school;

and "goal" (*qu*), meaning the destination toward which that tenet leads. However, this comprises both a general and a specific dimension. The general refers to the entirety of the Dharma-period teachings (*shijiao*); the specific, however, takes only [a particular portion].
In this sutra, regarding the comprehensive [teachings], there are many categories when examining all the various doctrines; they are not cited here at length.
Now, based on the general intent, I shall briefly clarify the fundamental purpose and outline the general principles of the provisional and the real within the teachings of the five periods.

Now, the provisional vehicle (*prajñapti-yāna*) is accomplished through multiple stages of cultivation; its movement manifests cause and effect, such that the cause is the essence (*tattva*) and the fruit is the goal (*gati*).
The perfect reality (*pūrṇa-tattva*) possesses nature inherently across multiple layers; its value lies in awakening and entry, such that awakening is the essence and entry is the goal.
If this sutra were to be taken generally as a teaching of the class of perfect reality to determine its essence and goal, then it would take awakening as [the essence].
Taking the clarification of the mind-ground as its primary tenet (*śāstra*) and the realization of the fruit-ground as its goal (*prayojana*), this is a brief elucidation of its general outline.

△ However, within that specific context, the meanings are vast and manifold, making it difficult to describe them all in detail. For now, we shall restrict ourselves to defining the primary tenets and goals of this specific sutra.

These also have both general and specific aspects. The general aspect refers to taking faith and understanding of the Great Samādhi as the tenet, and the cultivation and realization of the ultimate fruit as the goal.

This is for the sake of the audience. It is precisely because the audience requested the subtle *śamatha* and other methods that the World-Honored One revealed the Tathāgata-garbha mind as the inherently endowed, perfectly interfused Great Samādhi; is this not the central tenet of this sutra?
The audience wished to request how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi, and the World-Honored One showed them the entry into the Tathāgata.
The Ocean of Sublime Adornments is the fulfillment of Bodhi, returning to the state of non-attainment; this is precisely the ultimate fruit of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Is this not the destination toward which this single sutra tends? If one clarifies its specific meanings, there are six pairs:

namely, breaking and manifesting, partial and complete, awakening and entry, essence and function, practice and stage, and partial and full. In all these cases, the former represents the primary tenet (*mūla*) and the latter represents the final destination (*niṣṭhā*). Furthermore...

All of these tread upon the path of the preceding [section] as their approach, yet establish the principle of the subsequent [section] as their core, thereby giving rise to that approach once more. First, "Refutation and Revelation":

This refers to taking the critical refutation of the conscious mind as the core principle and the manifestation of the fundamental nature of the sense organs as the approach. That is to say, it involves a thorough refutation of false consciousness;
the intent lies in abandoning false consciousness while placing trust in and recognizing the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth. Second, "The Partial and the Total."

This means that it specifically takes the faculty-nature (*indriya-svabhāva*) as its primary subject (*mūla*) and fully reveals the storehouse-nature (*ālaya-svabhāva*) as its ultimate goal (*prayojana*).

This constitutes the tenfold demonstration, which specifically clarifies the seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddhi*). Its intent lies in expanding and fulfilling one's understanding and awakening, proceeding from the near to the far;

thus, by synthesizing the four categories and traversing the seven elements, everything is entirely returned to the storehouse-nature. Regarding the "threefold entry into realization," this refers to perfectly realizing the jeweled hall as...

The Thesis: To enter deeply through the gates is the goal. This also builds upon the previous [section] to fully reveal the nature of the treasury; it is precisely the perfect awakening to the flowered mansion.
However, the reason one must seek this perfect awakening to the flowered mansion lies in the intention to attain the single gate of universal penetration (*yuan-tong*).
From the initial entry into the stream and forgetting the object of perception, it proceeds directly until quiescence manifests before one. Regarding the four aspects of essence and function:

this means taking the realization of the perfect essence as the primary principle (*zong*) and the manifestation of the perfect function as the goal (*qu*). This also follows upon the previous gate for further penetration.

One immediately realizes this essence. However, the purpose of necessarily realizing this essence is to bring forth the great sovereign functions, such as the thirty-two transformations of perfect penetration.
Regarding the "five practices and stages," this means taking the practice of perfect concentration as the primary principle and traversing the stages of the perfect cause as the goal.
This also builds upon the aforementioned great functions to form a concise summary. Furthermore, there are two [aspects] to this: first—

The "Brief Account of Benefiting Sentient Beings" and the "Distinct Account of Attaining the Fruit" differ in their approach. In the former thirty-two chapters, only benefiting sentient beings is manifested while attaining the fruit remains implicit;
here, however, the practice of the Perfect [Teaching] is deployed precisely for the purpose of attaining the fruit.

Yet, the reason one must deploy the practice of the Perfect is that the intent lies in traversing all fifty-five stages of the perfect cause. Regarding the "six divisions being fulfilled," this refers to traversing the stages of partial realization of the holy positions.
This constitutes the primary tenet. Taking the attainment of perfect enlightenment as the goal, this also refers to the stage of the complete cause, which is the stage of partial realization.
The statement that one must necessarily pass through this stage is intended to mean the fulfillment of perfect enlightenment.

All of these arise from perfect faith and give rise to perfect understanding; they result in perfect realization through perfect practice. Thus, the essential purport of the entire scripture is as clear as pointing at one's own palm.
What is called the "perfect fusion of the gradual" is the non-obstruction of these two.

Regarding the sequence of the traces of the seven teachings: it is truly because the language and phrasing of this sutra are profound and its principles are subtle and deep, like a dragon amidst the clouds—appearing and disappearing, hidden and manifest, with its beginning and end impossible to fathom. Therefore, throughout the past and present, there have been various commentaries and interpretations concerning it.

The debates have been so convoluted that later students are left without a fundamental basis upon which to rely. In this commentary on the traces of the Buddhist teachings, I shall first open with two points:
first, a general account of past and present; second, a definitive determination of their chronological sequence. Regarding the first, the general account:

I humbly observe that while the various masters of past and present differ widely in their judgments regarding the timing [of the Buddha’s appearance], each possesses their own insights and is not without supporting evidence. It is for this reason that there are differing judgments.
Regarding those who place the *Lotus Sūtra* after the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are those such as Changqing Zhenji, Changshui, Gushan, Letan, and Jiaoguang.

There are also those who, like the previous [opinion], provide a definitive chronological judgment, asserting that this sūtra was preached in the forty-ninth year and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in the fiftieth year;
this is the view of Gushan. Furthermore, there are those who judge the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to be after and the *Lotus Sūtra* to be before; this is the view of Wenling.
There are those who judge it to be a later portion of the Vaipulya (fangděng). This is the interpretation of Shenzhi.

Others say that according to the rules for classification and inclusion established by our own school, although it is not subsumed within the four periods (sìshí), everything may be gathered under the Vaipulya. This is the view of Baiting Yue.

It is simply that the deeds recorded in the root sūtra appear either before or after [other teachings] across the various periods; this is what conforms [to one period] while that is what contradicts [another]. (Jiǎ)

Second, the refutation of the lack of a definitive conclusion. Furthermore, there are those who attempt to harmonize these points through forced interpretation, claiming that while the causal conditions for the teaching existed in the past, its actual initiation occurred in the present;
that the manifestation of its traces took place during the period of the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras, while the retrospective narration was recorded after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is the seal of the Tiantai school. Others say: "This scripture encompasses the five periods and penetrates the five teachings; it is judged to belong to the Esoteric division. This is not so.
As for determining the time and the teaching: it is Hanshan Deqing. The above has been a brief clarification and general exposition.
△ Next, regarding the determination [of the specific context]: this refers to what Changshui stated—that when the Buddha preached this sutra, he did not do so all at once.

The teachings necessarily have a sequence. As for their compilation, they are categorized by type and consolidated into a single collection. This refers to when the Buddha first spoke: King Bimbisāra was present in the assembly;
the Buddha recounted how outsiders had raised doubts, and thereby eliminated [the king's] view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Later, Ānanda arrived and questioned about the seven destinies, citing the case of Virūḍhaka’s slaughter of the Śākyas and Sunakṣatra’s preaching of emptiness—both of whom, while still alive, fell into hell. Was Virūḍhaka not...?
The son of King Ajātaśatru succeeded his father upon the king’s death and was then about to execute the Śākya clan.
How could he have raised a question concerning a matter that had not yet manifested? Thus, we know that this sutra was not spoken at a single time;

this judgment is indeed correct and constitutes a sublime discourse for all eternity. Nevertheless, if one wishes to place this sutra entirely after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, then—
Furthermore, it seems there was a slight lack of thoroughness, which led to the debate at Wēnlíng. Now, by dividing the text into two parts—preceding and following—I shall open it into two chapters:
the first, "The Formal Request and the Formal Exposition," and the second, "The Repeated Request and the Repeated Exposition.

Thus, the formal exposition corresponds to the preceding part, while the repeated exposition corresponds to the following part; for the formal exposition is definitively situated prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is stated again that this [event] definitely took place after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This is based on the *Ratnāvadāna* (因緣經) and the *Śākyamuni-pūrvapraśasti* (釋迦譜), which record that on the day of the Buddha’s birth, eight kings of India gave birth to sons on the same day and each bestowed auspicious names upon them.
The crown prince of Śrāvastī was named Prasenajit; furthermore, he was established as crown prince on that same day. In the present sūtra, King Prasenajit requests the Dharma. From...

The preface states that his age was sixty-two; thus, the Buddha’s age was likewise. This was thirty-two years after his attainment of enlightenment, precisely the time when he should have turned the wheel of teaching and preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it was at Jetavana that he preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and this marks the point where its exposition was nearing completion.
Moreover, Bodhiruci’s *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-śāstra* records the Buddha saying: "After my attainment of enlightenment..."

He preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for forty-two years. If one examines this according to the sūtras and śāstras, the actual teaching must have occurred after the *Prajñāpāramitā* period and before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This is because, although the study of wisdom (*prajñā*) had been manifested following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was not yet fully established;
therefore, the Tathāgata revealed the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama* to support that profound wisdom of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. He wished to...
When one cultivates both samādhi and wisdom equally, and when both understanding and practice are perfected, then the myriad practices of the secret cause will reach their ultimate consummation.
Reaching this state of total perfection and subtlety, there is no further need for cultivation. Therefore, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the Buddha spoke exclusively of the wondrous Dharma;

according to the capacities of those present, he granted his seal of approval and bestowed predictions of their future Buddhahood. Thus, the Great Matter—the original intent for which the Tathāgata appeared in the world—was brought to completion. Therefore...
That sutra states: "After a short time had passed, the father knew that his son’s mind was gradually becoming open and at ease;

thus, what were called 'correct requests' and 'correct explanations' were merely talk for that brief interval. Therefore, it is only this sutra that clarifies the refutation [of delusion] and the manifestation [of the stages].

After this, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, there are no further discussions regarding the sequence of stages (*avasthā*), nor any talk of refutation and manifestation. From this, one knows that [the teaching of] the correct...

It is said that [the first exposition] definitely occurred after the *Prajñāpāramitā* and before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for the subsequent re-exposition occurring after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it was because the assembly made specific requests:
Vimalakīrti and Sunaksatra extensively elucidated the seven destinies, and the World-Honored One, having returned, spoke of the five māras based on his own experience;
these were all instances of repeated requests and repeated expositions. This is confirmed by the fifty-ninth sutra of the *Madhyama Āgama*, where King Bimbisāra addresses [the Buddha].

The Buddha said: "I am eighty years old; thus the Tathāgata is also eighty. This is precisely the year when King Nimi abdicated his throne and Vairōcana usurped the father’s position and exterminated the Śākyas, and when Subhadra fell into prison—this is the causal origin of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Therefore, the *Śrī-amalavijaya-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching) states: The Buddha addressed Ānanda, 'After the Buddha has passed away, the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) is [the foundation]...'"
Therefore, O Great Master, in your current polemical writings you extensively slander the Vinaya discipline; this indeed belongs to Māra.
Furthermore, you claim that by following the Buddha’s words one repays the Buddha’s kindness—is this not precisely the intent of the earnest instructions and entrustments given at the Twin Trees?
Thus, from the very beginning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to its conclusion in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, sexual desire is identified as the affliction that disturbs and hinders [the path].
Since the divine mantra is revealed twice, this repetition must certainly be situated after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*;

of this there is no doubt. If one were to use this explanation to adjudicate among the various masters: Changshui’s division into "before" and "after" is truly lacking only in its connection to what precedes;
Wenzheng’s theory of "the early period" is indeed slightly deficient in its continuity with what follows. Thus, even Chang...
The masters Qingzhen, Jizhao, Gushan, Leduan, Tanjiao, Guangding, and others all judged that the *Lotus Sūtra* belongs to the later period.

However, one should not restrict this judgment to a single specific time. Thus, as the ancient worthies have said: "The times of exposition were not uniform; judgments differ between antiquity and the present.
My current attempt at harmonization differs somewhat from what was previously heard. I merely hope to clarify the meaning and do not dare to harbor dogmatic contention. Still...
I hope that Your Highness will graciously grant your approval.

Regarding the years of the eight translators, I have based this on the *Continued Record of the Illustrations of Translated Scriptures Past and Present* (Gujin yijing tujiji) compiled by Zhisheng during the Kaiyuan era.

This refers to a person from Central India of medium stature, whose Sanskrit name was Pramiti. He had carved out his own arm to conceal the scriptures and traveled across the sea to reach Guangzhou, where he stayed at Zhizhi Temple.
There he encountered the Chancellor Fang Rong, who had been exiled to Lingnan; hearing that this scripture existed there, [he sought it out].
He then wished to request a translation. The Master brought it forth; however, because it had been hidden for a long time, it was difficult to read due to the congealing of blood.
Fǎróng’s wife cleared it with water, whereupon it finally became clearly visible. They immediately proceeded with the translation at Zhìzhì Temple.

Thus, Míjiā served as the oral interpreter, Huáidi verified the translation, and Fángxiàng performed the pen-recording. This took place in the fifth month of the first year of the Shénlóng era of the Great Táng.

It was the twenty-third day of the month. However, as this scripture belongs to the *Abhiṣeka* (Consecration) section and had been extracted for separate practice, he completed the translation of its full extent and immediately returned to his country.
Because that king’s strict decree prohibited this scripture from being privately exported beyond the borders, it was kept secret as a national treasure.
Since the Master had secretly concealed and brought it across, he could not avoid being punished at the frontier. For...

To resolve this difficulty, he quickly returned. Furthermore, when Fang Xiang submitted his memorial via a southern envoy, it coincided with the beginning of Emperor Zhongzong’s reign over the great mandate;
as the state was beset by many affairs, there was no leisure to proclaim [the teachings].

At that time, the Chan Master Shenxiu, while at the Inner Court of the Daochang, happened to see the manuscript of the memorial and subsequently transcribed it for himself. He then carried it back to Dumen Monastery in Jingzhou.
Later, during the Northern Wei dynasty, the Venerable Zhen of Beiguantao, out of deep admiration for this scripture, searched for its sacred traces.
It was only at Du-men Monastery that he finally obtained this manuscript and began to establish its topical divisions (*kōpān*).

This constitutes the general account of the origins and history of this scripture, as well as the approximate date of its translation. △ Nine: General Explanation of the Title (2) 1. The Title of the Scripture.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Now, regarding this single sūtra, the Buddha spoke five titles; however, the translator has preserved three and concealed two in the heading, doing so to encompass the vast within the concise.
Thus, the expressive words and the expressed meaning together amount to only twenty characters. First, let us clarify the initial point.
That which is explained consists of nineteen characters. If categorized according to their textual meaning, they should be divided into general and specific aspects.

The three characters above clarify the general characteristic of the essence of the Dharma; the sixteen characters below provide a detailed exposition of the wondrous function of its specific characteristics.

Now, first, we shall clarify the general aspect, briefly providing two interpretations: first, the interpretation according to phenomena (*sūtra-vastu*); second, the interpretation entering into principle (*tattva*). First, the interpretation according to phenomena:
The term "Great" (*dà*) is a word of praise; it means, "How great is the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-śrī-vidyā*!
It is also a general title used for praise, while the following section beginning with "the secret cause" (*mì yīn*) details its specific meanings. If these are distinguished individually:

the "secret cause" is the Great Cause, the "definitive meaning" (*liǎoyì*) is the Great Meaning, the "ten thousand practices" (*wàn xíng*) are the Great Practice, and the *Śrī-mahā-sannipāta* (or *Śrī-vidyā*) is the Great [Dharma].
It is settled. By possessing these various "Greats," one can sufficiently know that this sutra is a Great Teaching.

That being so, those who wish to achieve Bodhi—can they not rely upon the Great Teaching to give rise to great faith, accord with the Great Principle to develop great understanding, awaken to the Great Principle to initiate great practice, and perfect great practice to realize the Great Fruit? Therefore, as for the meaning of "Great," it has not yet...
It is difficult to exhaustively explain this. That which is called "Buddha" is the Sanskrit term *buddha*. This means "awakened";

it refers to one who has awakened themselves and awakened others, whose practice of awakening is perfected, and is thus termed a Buddha. As for the term "Crown" (*ding*), it refers to the mark of the invisible crown among the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Situated amidst the blue-black curls of hair, it is like the sun emerging from a spring mountain.
This is indeed so. As for the title "One Whose Crown Cannot Be Seen," this refers to what is described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

immediately upon his birth, [the gods] held him up and gazed intently at him, yet could not see the crown of his head. Furthermore, the *Vajrapāṇi-rahasya-guhya-sūtra* states that after the Buddha attained enlightenment...
While traveling in Vārāṇasī, there was a bodhisattva from the east named Ādhāraṇa who came to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet.

Desiring to measure the Buddha’s body, he traveled by the Buddha’s supernatural power to worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the zenith, yet he could not see the crown of Śākyamuni’s head.

He went to inquire about the Lotus World, and that Buddha replied: "Even if one were to pass through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still could not see the crown of the head of Śākyamuni Buddha.
According to this sutra, it is clear that the Great Buddha-Crown possesses the meaning of being invisible.
Next, regarding the entry into principle: the Great Buddha-Crown is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), which constitutes the three [aspects] of the single mind.
"Great" (*mahat*) is an alternative designation for the Dharmakāya. "Great" refers directly to the human Dharmakāya, receiving its name from its very essence.
Because this essence pervades the entire Dharma-realm, encompassing all phenomena; it extends vertically through the three periods of time and horizontally across the ten directions;
